assessment.nobel_worthiness: Predicted flat bands at a magic twist angle, then observed correlated insulators and superconductivity in 2018. Prediction followed by clear clues from nature, which is what I look for. It opened moire and twistronics as a new field and has had very large impact in a short time.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the theoretical prediction (2011) and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive experimental discovery. This is a natural theory-plus-experiment configuration. Others (e.g. Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young, Yacoby, and earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) have claims that would need weighing.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups across graphene and TMD moire systems. Timing is early, about eight years, but the field is mature enough and the discovery is clear.
uncertainties: Priority of the earlier continuum-model work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is not within the credited names and is unresolved.
Whether the origin of the superconductivity is settled is something I cannot verify myself; this does not seem to affect the discovery itself.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, is a major advance in precision measurement. It gives fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and tests of fundamental constants and relativity, with prospects for redefining the second. The invention is clean and its consequences are concrete.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first clocks. Ye led the strontium clocks at the highest precision and with the greatest stability. Two laureates is a plausible configuration, though others (e.g. Lemonde, Schmidt, Wineland for ion clocks) may be raised.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by many laboratories worldwide, with comparisons across continents. The redefinition of the second is pending, so recognition is timely but the final application is not complete.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes (Hall and Hänsch 2005, Wineland 2012) may limit how novel the committee views the contribution.
The precise decisive contributions of Katori versus Ye and other lattice clock groups are not fully settled in my own knowledge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of X-ray, optical and radio afterglows of gamma-ray bursts in 1997 settled the cosmological distance of GRBs, one of the major puzzles in astrophysics. It established GRBs as the most luminous explosions in the universe and opened a new probe of the early universe. It is a clear discovery with clues from nature.
assessment.attribution: Costa and Frontera led the BeppoSAX detection of the X-ray afterglow, giving accurate positions. Kulkarni's group secured the optical, radio and redshift follow-up that confirmed the extragalactic origin. The three-person structure is plausible, though van Paradijs, Djorgovski, Metzger and Frail also have significant claims.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed over nearly three decades by Swift, Fermi and many follow-up studies. It is clearly mature, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Several other contributors (van Paradijs, Groot, Djorgovski, Frail, Piro) have claims that cannot be easily dismissed, and van Paradijs has died.
I am recalling the detailed sequence of events from memory and have not verified it.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, followed by its observation in HgTe quantum wells, created a new class of topological matter. It has strong conceptual originality and wide impact, including on later topological materials work.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the theoretical prediction, and Molenkamp's group did the experimental observation with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang's HgTe proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, along with Fu, Moore and Balents, Hasan and others, are not in the credited names, so allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent experiments (Bi2Se3 and others by ARPES). The field is mature and timing is appropriate.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe prediction (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and the 3D topological insulator (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hasan) is disputed and cannot be resolved by the supplied names.
Overlap with the Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz prize of 2016 might make the committee consider the topic partly rewarded.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution gives a communication method whose security rests on physical principles rather than computational assumptions. The BB84 protocol is a clear and original invention with a large field growing from it, and it ties quantum foundations to practice.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard's BB84 protocol is the central invention. Ekert's entanglement-based E91 protocol is an important separate contribution, so a three-person prize is conceivable. Wiesner's earlier conjugate coding is a further priority issue.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally demonstrated over fibre and satellite links, and commercial systems exist. Practical security and device-independence issues remain, but the principle is stable.
uncertainties: Whether Ekert should be included over one of the others is a real committee question.
Wiesner's unpublished conjugate coding priority is unresolved, and he is not credited.
The question of whether this is physics or computer science and information theory may arise.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP mapped the cosmic microwave background with the precision that established the standard Lambda-CDM model and fixed the age, composition and geometry of the universe. It is a decisive observation that directly addresses dark energy and dark matter, which are subjects close to my own interests.
assessment.attribution: Bennett led the mission, Page was key to the instrument and Spergel to the cosmological analysis. WMAP was a large collaboration, so choosing three people is difficult and contentious, as is the overlap with the COBE and Peebles prizes.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed and refined by Planck. The Lambda-CDM interpretation is stable although tensions such as the Hubble constant remain. Recognition has not yet been given although the results are old.
uncertainties: Allocation of credit in a large collaboration beyond three names is unclear.
The Planck mission may be seen as the more precise successor, which would complicate the case.
Overlap with the earlier Nobel prizes in cosmology (2006, 2011, 2019) is a concern.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's discovery of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos in 2013, and later the evidence for TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, opened neutrino astronomy. It gives new clues from nature about the sources of cosmic rays.
assessment.attribution: Halzen is the driving person behind the IceCube concept and its realization. This is only a single name and a large collaboration did the work; Nobel rules and fairness question whether one person can stand for it. Other pioneers of neutrino telescopes (e.g. the AMANDA and Baikal teams, and Markov) could be considered.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is firmly established and the source identification is now emerging, though the origin of most of the flux is still unknown. Recognition is probably somewhat early.
uncertainties: The list gives only one credited name, so any prize would leave out colleagues, such as the collaboration leadership.
The sources of most of the neutrinos are not identified, so the discovery could be seen as incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of the baryon acoustic peak in galaxy clustering in 2005 provided a standard ruler for dark energy and independent confirmation of cosmic acceleration. It ties into the question of dark energy that interests me and has since become a core cosmological probe, with newer DESI results hinting at possible evolving dark energy.
assessment.attribution: Eisenstein (SDSS) and Cole (2dFGRS, Percival) made nearly simultaneous independent detections; the 2dF and SDSS teams were large collaborations. Two prediction-side contributions (Peebles and Yu, Sunyaev and Zeldovich) are not on the list. A three-person split is not obviously fair.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many surveys (SDSS-III BOSS, eBOSS, DESI). The method is mature, but the physical interpretation of dark energy is still under active debate, and recent DESI results are not settled.
uncertainties: The role of early theory (Peebles and Yu; Sunyaev and Zeldovich) is not in the credited names.
It is a precision tool more than a single discovery, and the committee might view it as a measurement technique.
The recent DESI hints are unconfirmed and my knowledge may not be complete.
